summary: Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial protein synthesis and is active against gram-positive cocci (including many MRSA) and anaerobes. Systemic oral and IV/IM forms treat serious skin and soft tissue, intra-abdominal, bone/joint, gynecologic, and anaerobic infections, while the 1% topical form treats acne vulgaris. Its major safety concern is Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis, which can be severe and fatal. It also has useful antitoxin (protein synthesis suppression) activity in toxin-mediated syndromes.
indications: Serious skin and soft tissue infections including those caused by streptococci, staphylococci (incl. MRSA), and anaerobes (systemic)
Anaerobic infections (intra-abdominal, gynecologic, aspiration pneumonia, lung abscess)
Bone and joint infections (often as adjunct/oral step-down)
Adjunct for toxin-mediated disease (necrotizing fasciitis, streptococcal/staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome) for toxin suppression

admin: Topical: apply a thin film twice daily to the affected area; for external use only; shake lotion before use and avoid eyes, mouth, and broken skin
Oral: take capsules with a full glass of water to minimize esophageal irritation; may be taken with or without food
IV: dilute and infuse over at least 10-60 minutes; never administer undiluted as an IV bolus
IV infusion rate should not exceed 30 mg/min, and no more than 1200 mg in a single 1-hour infusion

Keep all liquid dosage forms tightly closed; protect topical lotion from freezing
moa: Clindamycin inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding to the 23S RNA of the 50S ribosomal subunit, preventing peptide bond formation. It is generally bacteriostatic but bactericidal at higher concentrations against susceptible organisms. By halting protein synthesis it also suppresses production of bacterial exotoxins, which underlies its adjunctive role in toxin-mediated infections.

relative: History of regional enteritis or ulcerative colitis (per topical label contraindication; use systemic with great caution)
First trimester of pregnancy unless clearly needed
monitor: CBC and liver/renal function on prolonged therapy
Enhanced neuromuscular blockade when combined with such agents

preg: Systemic clindamycin in the second and third trimesters has not been associated with increased congenital abnormalities in clinical trials. There are no adequate first-trimester studies, so use during the first trimester only if clearly needed.
lact: Orally and parenterally administered clindamycin appears in breast milk and may affect the breastfed infant's GI flora (diarrhea, candidiasis, or rarely bloody stool from antibiotic-associated colitis). Weigh benefits of breastfeeding against maternal need; monitor the infant. If topical lotion is applied to the chest, avoid accidental infant ingestion.
renal: No routine dosage adjustment is required in renal impairment; clindamycin is not appreciably removed by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis.
hepatic: Clindamycin is extensively metabolized hepatically; serious hepatic impairment can prolong its half-life. Use with caution and monitor liver function and serum levels in severe hepatic dysfunction; dose reduction may be warranted.

major: Neuromuscular blocking agents - clindamycin may enhance neuromuscular blockade
Erythromycin / macrolides - antagonism (overlapping ribosomal binding); avoid co-administration
moderate: CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) - may increase clindamycin exposure
CYP3A4 inducers (e.g., rifampin) - may decrease clindamycin exposure
minor: Cross-resistance with lincomycin is complete; inducible cross-resistance with macrolides/streptogramin B possible
interactions.food: Oral absorption is essentially unaffected by food; take with a full glass of water.
interactions.alcohol: No specific clinically significant interaction with alcohol.
interactions.diagnostics: Avoid antiperistaltic agents (opiates, diphenoxylate-atropine) if diarrhea develops as they may worsen C. difficile colitis. Stool C. difficile toxin/culture and large-bowel endoscopy aid diagnosis of suspected pseudomembranous colitis.

common: Topical: burning, itching, dryness, erythema, peeling, oily skin
serious: Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea / pseudomembranous colitis (can occur weeks after stopping)
emergency: Fulminant / toxic megacolon from C. difficile colitis

Take oral capsules with a full glass of water and remain upright to avoid throat/esophageal irritation
Complete the entire prescribed systemic course even if you feel better

Shake the topical lotion before each use
Tell your doctor about any prior bowel disease or antibiotic allergy

pk: Rapid; therapeutic serum levels within ~45-60 min of oral dose (topical: minimal systemic absorption)
Oral peak ~45-60 min; IV peak at end of infusion
Approximately 2.4-3 hours (prolonged in severe hepatic/renal impairment)
Dosing every 6-8 hours maintains therapeutic levels
Oral/topical at 20-25C (68-77F); do not refrigerate reconstituted oral solution; protect topical lotion from freezing
pearls: Excellent oral bioavailability (~90%) allows IV-to-oral step-down at the same dose for many infections
Add to beta-lactam in necrotizing soft tissue infection and toxic shock for anti-toxin (Eagle effect) protein-synthesis suppression
One of the highest-risk antibiotics for C. difficile colitis - reserve and counsel patients
Good activity against many community-acquired MRSA, but check local D-test for inducible clindamycin resistance (erm-mediated)
Topical 1% has negligible systemic absorption (serum 0-3 ng/mL, <0.2% urinary recovery), yet rare colitis still reported
Antagonistic with erythromycin/macrolides - do not co-administer
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule - do not double up. For topical use, apply when remembered unless it is nearly time for the next application.
overdose: Systemic overdose is managed supportively as there is no specific antidote; clindamycin is not effectively removed by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. Monitor for and manage hypersensitivity and GI/colitis effects. Topically applied clindamycin can be absorbed in amounts sufficient to produce systemic effects, including diarrhea/colitis. Discontinue the drug and provide fluid/electrolyte support; if C. difficile colitis develops, treat with oral vancomycin (500 mg to 2 g/day in 3-4 divided doses for 7-10 days) or fidaxomicin and avoid antiperistaltic agents.
